title: Noah and the Flood
english: The one who has remembered well the laws regarding piety and justice is not unworthy of being a judge. However, those who were named wise by others were actually the last and youngest, having stolen the ideas of their predecessors and incorporated them into their own words. Although they did not entirely succeed, they gained a reputation for speaking nobly and seeming to speak the truth. There were some who came after Moses, and others who lived at various times with the holy prophets after him. Those who followed their glory were deemed worthy of the superior vote by the others, even though they did not entirely free the glory of God from falsehood.

Moses, the oldest, was first in time, but those who came after him were last. To understand this, one should approach the reading and the list of names, or the count of times, with diligence and a strong desire for the assurance that comes with each. Noah, a man especially loved by God, was the tenth from the first, Adam. God commanded him to build an ark, because a flood was going to destroy everything on earth, and to enter it with his wife, sons, and various kinds of animals, birds, and reptiles, and to sail through it. This story, alluded to in Genesis 6-9, serves as a reminder of God's power and providence.

When the flood had finally subsided, the entire human race and all the other animals were destroyed, but Noah's household was saved. The ark came to rest on the mountains of Ararat, in the region of Armenia. After the flood, Noah made a sacrifice to God, expressing his gratitude for his salvation. The Scripture, inspired by God, is a trustworthy account of these events.

Some people, however, consider our accounts to be mere myths, devoid of any historical basis. Nevertheless, I must also mention the historians of other nations, such as Alexander Polyhistor and Abydenus, who have written about these events in their own works. Although their accounts may not be entirely accurate, they do provide some insight into the flood and its aftermath. According to Alexander, after the death of Otiartes, his son Xisuthros reigned for 18 years, during which time the great flood occurred. Xisuthros was saved because Cronus had warned him about the flood and told him to build a boat and sail in it with birds, reptiles, and animals. Abydenus gives a clearer account, saying that after the death of Otiartes, Xisuthros and others became rulers, and Cronus warned Xisuthros about the flood and told him to hide all written records in the city of the Sun in Sippar. Xisuthros did this and then sailed to Armenia, where he was taken up by God.

After the rain had stopped on the third day, a trial was made with the birds to see if they could find dry land. The birds, having been released from the invisible sea, wandered and were carried back to the ark, with others accompanying them. The third group was fortunate, as the gods made the one who had stuck his feet in the mud invisible to humans.

The ark was located in Armenia, where it provided wooden amulets to the local population. The name Xisuthrus is believed to be another name for Noah, possibly due to the Assyrian pronunciation. However, this is an error, as the name Cronus was used instead of the God of all, which is not surprising given that they did not participate in the divine light and did not see the holy beauty of truth with the eyes of their mind.

According to the Sibyl, when all people had the same voice, some of them decided to build a very large tower to ascend to heaven. However, God sent winds to destroy the tower, and as a result, each person was given their own unique voice. This event is said to be the origin of the city of Babylon. Abideneus offers a similar account, stating that the first people, filled with pride and a sense of their own strength and size, attempted to build a tower to reach heaven, but the winds destroyed it, and the city was left in ruins.

After the people were scattered, Ninus, the son of Arbel, became the first king of the Assyrians, and his city, Nineveh, was built by Semiramis. Meanwhile, Abraham, a wise and knowledgeable man, sought to know the truth and the creator of all things. He was determined to understand the nature of the universe and the one who had created it. God, seeing Abraham's desire for knowledge and his commitment to seeking the truth, called him to leave his family and go to a land that He would show him. Abraham's journey was just beginning, and he would soon discover the true nature of his creator and the purpose of his existence.

As I reflect on my life and the many events that have transpired, I must pass over the details for now, as our discussion necessarily turns to other matters of the time. In tracing the timeline from Abraham to Moses, we find that Moses was born in Egypt, where the descendants of Abraham had settled, in the four hundred and twentieth year after the divine Abraham. Moses, while still young, was trained in Egyptian wisdom, which served as a kind of preliminary exercise for the divine things he would later encounter.

The stories of old tell us that in the seventh year of Moses' life, Prometheus and Epimetheus, as well as Atlas and Argus, were born. Later, in the thirty-fifth year of Moses, Cecrops, the double-natured, became the first king of Athens, and he is said to have been the first to sacrifice an ox and to have named Zeus the highest of the gods among the Greeks. The flood in the time of Deucalion is also said to have occurred in the sixty-seventh year of Moses, and in Ethiopia, Phaethon, the son of Helios, was consumed by fire. Furthermore, in the seventy-fourth year of Moses, Hellen, the son of Deucalion and Pyrrha, became the origin of the name 'Hellenes' for the Greeks. Finally, in the one hundred and twentieth year of Moses, Dardanus founded the city of Dardania, while various rulers held power in different regions.

Egypt was also the name of Danos' brother. In the one hundred sixtieth year after Moses, Cadmus of Thebes reigned, and his daughter Semele was the mother of Dionysus, according to their accounts. The musicians Linus the Theban and Amphion were also present.

Phineas, the son of Eleazar and grandson of Aaron, succeeded to the priesthood among the Hebrews after Aaron's death. In the one hundred ninety-fifth year after Moses, the Greeks say that Kore was abducted by Hades, who was king of the Molotti at the time. Hades was said to have raised a massive dog, Cerberus, which he left to Perithus and Theseus when they arrived to abduct his wife. Then, something was corrupted…

title: The Oneness and Transcendence of God in Abrahamic Faith
english: After the ancient Egyptian way of life, after the mythologized age of gods and heroes, they say they first employed written laws to persuade the multitude—a man great in soul and in life, the newest among those remembered by the Jews, Moses, the one called God. Indeed, because he was found full of every virtue, they deified Moses and called him God, honoring him, I believe, some of those in Egypt, or perhaps having learned elsewhere what was said to him by the God over all. Behold, I have given you as God to Pharaoh.

Therefore, I think, regarding antiquity, and indeed that the wisdom esteemed among the Greeks antedates Moses and claims greater age, our argument has exhausted its point, possessing irrefutable and clear proof. It is necessary, then, that we Hebrews now engage in debate over the opinion we hold concerning God and the world’s origin or formation, and subsequently present what the wise Greeks have judged to be evident, setting it forth clearly for those who approach.

For in regard to the words of divinely inspired Scripture, those who hold them perceive themselves to be better and agree with one another. But each one of their own inventions renders things differently, and being intoxicated with foreign opinions, they easily demonstrate this divergence. For it was not at all possible to resist the things above mind and word within us, unless by the all-ruling God, who brings light into the mind, endows wisdom, finds tongue, and imparts something of the secret things concerning him, according to the local place, urging them both to understand and to speak.

Would that this grace were not poured out without distinction upon everyone, but rather given especially to those who have been cleansed of carnal and earthly defilements, who are sound in mind and skilled in the works of piety and virtue. And to this very point the God of all addresses us through the voice of David: 'Be still and know that I am God, and moreover the Lord our Jesus Christ.' Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God. Thus the transcendent nature would be perceived not by the bodily eyes, but by the inward eyes of the mind, subtle and precise in its inquiry, and the imaginations that reach beyond sense drawing to themselves the radiant beams of theophany.

Thus those who lived from Adam until Noah, having come into existence as men, worshipped one God, the true Creator and Lord of all by nature. No one has been inclined toward turning to other gods or to unclean demons. But after the flood and the construction of the tower and the division of tongues, they too have embraced an incompatible doctrine of God, those who have been scattered over the earth. For having abandoned the truth and given their minds over to temporal and earthly pursuits and bodily pleasures, they have rushed into every extreme of error, and as it were apportioned among themselves the transgressions of polytheistic delusion.

I believe Moses himself would be enough for us on this point, since he was Abraham’s descendant and shared his mindset; he not only thought as Abraham did but also judged it worthy to pass on in writing. The author of Genesis then relates how some had plundered the Sodomites and taken captives, including Lot, and rejoiced as if victorious, yet their hope was misled by Abraham’s unexpected attack and rescue of those who had been seized. After returning from the defeat of the five kings, as the text records, the king of Sodom approached him and said, 'Give me the people, but keep the goods for yourself.' Abraham, however, refused to accept any reward for his virtuous action, declaring instead, 'I raise my hand to the Lord, God Most High, maker of heaven and earth, and swear that if I take so much as a shoelace or a sandal-thong from you, it shall not be said that I have enriched Abraham.' He thus treated the possessions as devoted to destruction, lest anyone credit his wealth to the king of Sodom. Then Melchizedek, king of Salem, came forth and blessed him, saying, 'Blessed be Abraham by God Most High, creator of heaven and earth, and blessed be God Most High, who has delivered your enemies into your hand.' Later, Abraham sent his trusted servant, or one of his loyal household staff, into the region of the rivers to find a wife for Isaac, and he exacted an oath, saying, 'I adjure you by the God of heaven and the God of earth.'

This passage shows how Abraham’s faith was affirmed not by riches but by divine blessing, and how his refusal of the king’s offer preserved the integrity of his vocation. The writer emphasizes that Abraham’s victory was not measured in material gain but in spiritual fidelity, and that his subsequent actions—especially in securing Isaac’s marriage—were undertaken under solemn religious obligation. The repeated invocation of God as possessor of heaven and earth underscores the theological consistency from Melchizedek’s blessing to the servant’s oath, linking creation, redemption, and covenant purpose in a single narrative arc.
Abraham, the divinely inspired patriarch, clearly affirmed that there is only one God. He called God the Most High and the Maker of all things, both in heaven and on earth.

Therefore, the height of God is not perceptible, nor is it conceived as existing in a place, nor is it anything that one could grasp in bodily form; but it is to stand exalted above all things in a manner befitting God, and it is from Him that the things in the heavens and the things on the earth were made, and even the firmament itself, and indeed the earth too, I say, is that elemental substance.

If all things came into being through Him, then necessarily there is something else that is distinct from all things, and distinct according to nature, since He is neither begotten nor comes from non-existence, but is unbegotten and moreover eternal, the most ancient of all time, and the origin of all things.
